01What a vector is

Definition

Vector: a quantity that describes a magnitude and a direction.

– represent vectors using arrows, denoted bold letter:     v  

↳ length indicates magnitude, direction by arrow.

Two vectors are equal (or equivalent) when they have same magnitude and same direction.

The zero vector has magnitude zero and no direction.

Explanation (added)

In print (Stewart) vectors are bold, ; by hand you cannot write bold, so an arrow goes on top, . The key consequence of the definition of equality is that a vector has no fixed position: you may slide it anywhere, as long as you do not turn it or stretch it. That freedom is what makes tip-to-tail addition possible.

Coordinatize vectors by placing tails at origin.

Typed note included in the PDF

Question asked: “why do we call it basis vector?”

Because everything else is built out of them. “Basis” in the ordinary sense — a foundation.

Two things have to be true for that word to be earned:

1. They reach everything. Any vector in 3-space can be written as . Nothing is out of reach — pick the right three coefficients and you can hit any arrow in space.

2. The way is unique. There’s exactly one set of coefficients that works for a given vector. is and nothing else. If there were two different ways to write the same vector, the components wouldn’t be well-defined, and the word “the -component” would be meaningless.

Together: reaches everything, exactly one way each. That’s a basis.

08Applications: forces and velocities

Force is represented by vectors.

If several forces are acting on an object, the resultant force is the vector sum of the forces.

Typed note included in the PDF

The setup. A boat (or swimmer) points straight across the river, capable of 5 m/s in still water. The current carries everything downstream at 2 m/s.

Put downstream and across:

That’s the green diagonal on his board — the parallelogram law, exactly the diagram from earlier. Both effects start at the same point; the sum is the diagonal.

Actual speed:

Actual direction — angle off the intended straight-across heading:

So you aim due north and arrive northeast of where you wanted. The boat’s heading and its course are different vectors.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • “Find and its length”, given two points; or “find , , ”.
  • “Find a unit vector in the same direction as …” (sometimes “a vector of length 6 in the direction of …”).
  • “Draw and ” from a picture of two arrows — triangle or parallelogram law.
  • A word problem: a boat or plane with a current or wind (find the true speed and direction), or a weight hanging from two wires at given angles (find both tensions).
